## University of Warwick

::: course
**Topics in Development Economics (EC310)**, 2025-26
[Course page](https://courses.warwick.ac.uk/modules/2025/EC310-15){.paper-link target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>Course content</summary>

This module looks at a range of economic problems in low-income countries. It shows how the tools of economic analysis, especially models of household behaviour, can explain economic behaviour and help design policies to address acute economic problems. Topics may include agricultural households, the behavioural aspects of poverty, culture, child labour, comparative development, the determinants of growth, education, firms, gender, health, institutions, labour markets, market failures and microfinance, poverty and inequality, and policy on issues such as migration and industrialisation.

</details>
:::

## London School of Economics

::: course
**Microeconomic Principles I (EC201)**, 2020-21

<details>
<summary>Course content</summary>

This is an intermediate course in microeconomic analysis. It gives a broad overview of economic principles, including some recent developments in thinking, and teaches students to apply the tools of microeconomics to concrete economic problems. The course starts with consumer theory, covering preferences and utility, demand, income and substitution effects and welfare analysis, with applications to savings and labour supply. It then moves on to behavioural economics and decision-making under risk, including expected utility, insurance and prospect theory. Producer theory covers production and cost functions, supply and market structure, and game theory is applied to oligopoly and auctions. Later topics include general equilibrium, efficiency and inequality, public goods and externalities, political economy, contracts under moral hazard and adverse selection, and innovation, along with the role of government in each.

</details>
:::

::: course
**Economics B (EC102)**, 2019-20

<details>
<summary>Course content</summary>

This is an introductory course in microeconomics and macroeconomics. The first half covers consumer and producer theory, markets and competition, welfare, game theory, and adverse selection and moral hazard. The second half covers how the aggregate economy is measured, growth and development, economic fluctuations, stabilisation policy, money and inflation, unemployment, and financial and sovereign crises.

</details>
:::
